articles.title: Youth Olympics 2026: Dhinidhi Desinghu wins India's first -ever swimming medal
articles.content: Youth Olympics 2026: Dhinidhi Desinghu wins India's first-ever swimming medal Dhinidhi Desinghu registered a personal best time to win bronze in girls' 100m freestyle. By : The Bridge Desk Update: 2026-11-02 15:46 GMT Dhinidhi Desinghu poses with her 2026 Youth Olympics bronze medal (Photo credit: Special Arrangement) Dhinidhi Desinghu bagged a bronze medal in girls' 100m freestyle to open India's medal tally at the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal on Monday. The 17-year-old from Bengaluru clocked a personal best and Best Indian time of 56.27s to finish on the podium at the Dakar Aquatic Centre. Dhinidhi, who was the youngest Indian in the Paris Olympics contingent two years ago, finished behind Ana Bobanovic of Croatia (55.89s) and Alyssa Lawson (56.13s) of New Zealand to take the third spot. The youngster clocked 27.31s to the first 50m split and was placed fifth before surging her way forward in the final 50m to win the medal. #News | India opens its medal tally at 2026 Youth Olympics😍🇮🇳🔥 Dhinidhi Desinghu bags a bronze medal in women's 100m freestyle, clocking a personal best and best Indian time of 56.27s🥉 This is India's first-ever medal in swimming at the Youth Olympics!👏 📸: Special Arrangement #Swimming #YouthOlympics — The Bridge (@the_bridge_in) November 2, 2026 Dhinidhi's exploits comes just a day after Tirthank Pegu finished just outside the podium in boys' 100m butterfly, finishing fourth and losing out on a historic medal by just 0.27s. Dhinidhi's medal win is now India's first-ever medal in swimming at the Youth Olympics, surpassing Pegu's fourth-place finish to become India's best-ever performance in the sport. Before the 2026 Youth Olympics got underway, the best Indian performance at the Games was a sixth-place finish for Srihari Nataraj during the 2018 Games in Buenos Aires, Argentina in Boys' 100m backstroke. articles.title: IIT Hyderabad, Crimson Energy complete inaugural nuclear technology programme
articles.content: NRI View Point cartoon My Space Reviews Education Today Property Lifestyle Home | Telangana | Iit Hyderabad Crimson Energy Complete Inaugural Nuclear Technology Programme IIT Hyderabad, Crimson Energy complete inaugural nuclear technology programme IIT Hyderabad and Crimson Energy Experts have completed the inaugural ANUGYAN nuclear technology programme, training 23 engineers and industry professionals over three months. The initiative aims to develop skilled manpower for India's expanding nuclear power sector and emerging technologies By Telangana Today Published Date - 2 November 2026, 06:54 PM Sangareddy : The Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad (IITH) and Crimson Energy Experts Private Limited (CEEPL) completed the inaugural batch of ANUGYAN – Nuclear Technology Orientation Programme (NTOP) at the IITH campus. A total of 23 engineers and industry professionals completed the three-month, fully residential programme, which commenced on August 3. Over twelve weeks, participants received structured training in reactor physics, thermal hydraulics, radiation shielding, Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), nuclear safety, quality assurance and the regulatory framework of the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB). The curriculum combined academic instruction with laboratory experiments, generic nuclear power plant simulator training, technical case studies and practical insights from experienced professionals associated with India’s nuclear establishment, including BARC and NPCIL. The programme was designed to bridge academic engineering education and the practical requirements of nuclear projects, equipping participants with an understanding of nuclear technologies, safety culture, quality standards and regulatory requirements. The successful completion of the inaugural batch marks an important milestone in industry–academia collaboration. With India pursuing its ambition of increasing nuclear power capacity from approximately 8.8 GWe towards 100 GWe by 2047, the demand for trained professionals across design engineering, manufacturing, construction, commissioning, operations, quality assurance and safety is expected to increase significantly. ANUGYAN aimed to address this need while supporting emerging technologies, including SMRs and microreactors. Chairperson of Central Electricity Authority (CEA) Ghanshyam Prasad said nuclear power will be an essential component of India’s clean, reliable and round-the-clock electricity supply as the country was advancing towards its 2047 goals. He said that realising India’s nuclear ambitions will require not only advanced technologies and infrastructure but also a strong pool of skilled professionals. Director of IITH Prof BS Murty said ANUGYAN was conceived to combine strong academic foundations with an understanding of the practical, technological, safety and regulatory requirements of the nuclear industry. articles.title: India's first indigenous bullet train to carry 557 passengers at 249 kmph - o Heraldo
articles.content: SHARE India’s first indigenous bullet train is being manufactured at the Bharat Earth Movers Limited (BEML) facility in Bengaluru for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail corridor. Designed by Indian engineers, the train is being developed to operate in the country’s climatic and operational conditions. The train is designed to reach a maximum test speed of 280 kmph, while its operational speed will be 249 kmph. Measuring 202 metres, it will feature eight coaches — four motor cars and four trailer cars — with a passenger capacity of 557, including two seats for persons with reduced mobility. - Advertisement - If you enjoyed reading this article, you can help support our journalism by adding OHeraldo as a preferred source. Seven coaches will have standard-class seating in a 3×2 configuration, while one executive-class coach will feature 2×2 seating. Driver’s cabs at both ends will be equipped with an intelligent on-board control system to support decision-making and coordination with the operation control centre. Two eight-coach trains can also be coupled to form a 16-coach formation for future operations. The train’s interiors are being designed for passenger comfort, with spacious seats, generous legroom and ergonomically tailored features suited to Indian passengers. Wide windows will provide views from every row, while LED lighting, overhead racks and dedicated floor-mounted luggage stands will offer convenience during travel. Individual power outlets will allow passengers to charge laptops and mobile devices. The train will also feature sealed, single-piece gangways between coaches, enabling passengers to move smoothly through the train. Modern bio-digester toilets are designed to minimise effluent impact. A passenger information system will provide updates through LCD displays in English, Hindi and regional languages. Public address and automatic announcement systems will also keep passengers informed. A high-speed Wi-Fi-based infotainment system will allow travellers to access preloaded entertainment, while emergency talk-back units in passenger cabins and vestibules will enable communication with train crew. - Advertisement - Accessibility features include level boarding, dedicated seating and doors and toilets designed for persons with reduced mobility. Retractable footsteps integrated into the doors will help reduce the gap between the train and platform. Braille-enabled signage will assist visually impaired passengers. To maintain comfort throughout the year, each coach will have a dual-unit heating, ventilation and air-conditioning system to regulate temperature and humidity. Sound insulation in the car body and floor structure, along with noise-damping coatings, will help reduce noise during the journey. The train will operate using a 25 kV AC overhead electrical system. Its regenerative braking system will capture energy when the train slows down and feed it back into the electrical grid, improving energy efficiency. Engineers have also used computer simulations to shape the train’s aerodynamic nose and body. The design aims to reduce wind resistance and turbulence, while limiting loud sonic-boom noises as the train passes through tunnels. - Advertisement - The indigenous train is being developed as a key component of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project, with features focused on speed, passenger comfort, accessibility and energy efficiency. articles.title: “280 Kmph, 557 Passengers”: India's First Indigenous Bullet Train Promises Speed, Comfort ...
articles.content: Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email Support Independent Journalism Support Goemkarponn’s mission for fearless journalism. Donate Now New Delhi: India is preparing to introduce its first indigenously designed high-speed bullet train, marking a major milestone in the country’s railway manufacturing capabilities. The eight-coach train is being manufactured at the Bharat Earth Movers Limited (BEML) facility in Bengaluru for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail corridor. Designed by Indian engineers to suit the country’s climatic and operational conditions, the train will have a maximum test speed of 280 kmph and an operational speed of 249 kmph. The 202-metre-long train will accommodate 557 passengers and comprise four motor cars and four trailer cars. Its configuration will include seven standard-class coaches with 3×2 seating and one executive-class coach with 2×2 seating. Two dedicated seats will be available for persons with reduced mobility. The train will feature driver’s cabins at both ends, equipped with an intelligent onboard control system to support communication and coordination with the operation control centre. Two eight-coach trains can also be coupled to operate as a 16-coach formation when required. Passenger Comfort and Modern Facilities The interiors have been designed to provide greater comfort, with spacious seating, generous legroom and wide windows offering scenic views. A sealed gangway connecting the coaches will allow passengers to move between compartments conveniently. Other facilities will include LED lighting, overhead luggage racks, dedicated storage for oversized baggage and individual power outlets for charging electronic devices. Modern bio-digester toilets will also be installed to minimise environmental impact. A dual-unit heating, ventilation and air-conditioning system in every coach will maintain comfortable temperature and humidity throughout the journey. Advanced Information and Accessibility Features Passengers will have access to LCD information displays providing updates in English, Hindi and regional languages. Automatic announcements, public address systems and Wi-Fi-based infotainment facilities will further improve the travel experience. Emergency communication units will be installed inside passenger compartments and vestibules to allow travellers to contact train crew members when required. The train will also feature level boarding, retractable footsteps, accessible toilets and Braille-enabled signage to assist passengers with reduced mobility and visual impairments. Energy Efficiency and Safety Technology Powered by a 25 kV AC overhead electrical system, the train will use regenerative braking technology to recover energy during deceleration and feed it back into the electrical grid. Its aerodynamic design has been developed using advanced computer simulations to reduce air resistance, turbulence and noise, particularly while passing through tunnels. Additional sound insulation and noise-damping materials will help provide a quieter journey. With its combination of indigenous manufacturing, modern technology and passenger-focused facilities, the train represents an important step in India’s ambition to establish a high-speed rail network. articles.title: NTPC to set up India's first ceramic-based project to generate solar power at night in ...
articles.content: The project will use ceramic thermal energy storage technology developed by US-based company 247Solar. Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Limited (RRECL) has approved NTPC to set up a 320 kW pilot concentrated solar power (CSP) project at Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan. The project will test ceramic-based thermal energy storage technology to generate electricity using solar energy stored during the day, including after sunset. The project aims to assess the possibility of generating solar power at night while reducing dependence on conventional battery storage. Electricity generated through the pilot project will be used for internal and auxiliary consumption at the NTPC plant. Tech development Under the proposed technology, solar energy captured during the day will be stored as heat in high-temperature ceramic modules. After sunset, the stored heat will be used to operate an air turbine and generate electricity. The project will use ceramic thermal energy storage technology developed by US-based company 247Solar. NTPC is working with RRECL to implement and test the technology at Bhadla. Following the approval, preliminary feasibility studies, site surveys and structural testing will be undertaken at the project site. Solar power generation after sunset remains a challenge because conventional solar photovoltaic plants depend on sunlight and require storage systems to supply electricity after generation hours. The pilot project will assess whether thermal storage using ceramic modules can provide an alternative to chemical battery-based storage. If the technology proves feasible, it could be considered for deployment at other solar power projects. The pilot will also provide data on its operational performance and suitability for integration with existing solar infrastructure.

articles.title: India's First Bullet Train Takes Shape: Railway Minister Reviews Manufacturing Progress
articles.content: *Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw reviewed the manufacturing of Bharat-made Bullet Train-B28 at ADITYA - manufacturing Facility in Bengaluru on November 1, 2026. Union Minister for Railways Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw has reviewed the manufacturing of the Bharat-made Bullet Train-B28 at the ADITYA manufacturing Facility in Bengaluru. The Minister, on November 1, reviewed the specialised manufacturing infrastructure, including precision-engineered jigs and fixtures for car-body fabrication, and witnessed key stages of production such as underframe, sidewall, roof assembly, car assembly, surface preparation, treatment, etc. These advanced manufacturing processes are critical to achieving the precision, strength and quality standards required for high-speed rail operations. He also witnessed the ‘Squeeze Test’ demonstration, a critical quality assurance process in which the train carbody is subjected to controlled compressive/tensile forces to assess its structural strength, rigidity and dimensional stability. He examined passenger seats, focusing on the comfort and convenience they will offer during high-speed journeys, and reviewed key onboard systems and components, including the Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system, couplers and other train equipment and assemblies. He, who is seen in the enclosed pictures, also reviewed side module and roof module manufacturing and witnessed the subsequent integration and assembly operations. articles.title: Assam to Set Up India's First Public-Sector Proton Therapy Centre - GKToday
articles.content: Home Assam to Set Up India’s First Public-Sector Proton Therapy Centre Assam to Set Up India’s First Public-Sector Proton Therapy Centre November 2, 2026 Current Affairs Today - Latest Current Affairs - 2026-2027 On 31 October 2026, the Assam government signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Belgium-based Ion Beam Applications (IBA) Particles to establish India’s first public-sector proton beam therapy centre at Gauhati Medical College and Hospital in Guwahati. Project funding and cancer-care plans The project is estimated to cost ₹600 crore. Funding includes a ₹315 crore World Bank loan and a ₹285 crore contribution from the Assam government. The centre is expected to become operational in at least three years. It will be India’s third proton beam therapy facility, after private centres at Tata Cancer Hospital in Mumbai and Apollo Hospital in Chennai. The initiative aims to make advanced cancer treatment, particularly for children, more accessible and affordable; private proton therapy can cost up to ₹50 lakh. The state cabinet approved the centre in August 2026 under the Assam State Secondary Healthcare Initiative for Service Delivery Transformation (ASSIST). Assam has 12 of its 17 planned cancer hospitals functional and is seeking to expand its cancer-care infrastructure. Important Facts for Exams Bragg-peak deposition: Proton beams deliver their maximum dose near the end of their range, with very few protons penetrating beyond that depth. Pencil-beam scanning: Pencil-beam scanning uses magnets to steer thin proton beamlets, painting the target layer by layer without apertures or compensators. Paediatric tissue sparing: For paediatric cancers, proton therapy’s minimal exit dose can limit radiation to surrounding normal tissues and reduce acute toxicity. articles.title: India's First Bullet Train B28: Speed, Features, Capacity and Specifications
articles.content: India is shifting closer to ushering in the era of high-speed rail travel with the development of its maiden indigenous bullet train, the B28, which is slated to be launched in August 2027. Built by BEML at its Aditya Plant in Bengaluru, the train is being developed for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail corridor. With a maximum testing speed of 280 kmph and an operational speed of 249 kmph, the B28 will revolutionise long-distance passenger travel in the country. Inside India’s First Bullet Train The eight-coach train will be approximately 202 metres long and accommodate around 557 passengers. Its key features include seven standard-class coaches with 3x2 seating and one executive-class coach with 2x2 seating. The train will also have four motor cars and four trailer cars. It can also be doubled with another eight-coach trainset to create a 16-coach configuration, increasing passenger capacity. The design especially emphasises passenger comfort and convenience. The coaches will possess ergonomic seating, spacious legroom, LED lighting, overhead luggage racks, power outlets and wide windows. Bio-digester toilets will also be offered. A modern heating, ventilation and air-conditioning system, with two units in every coach, will retain comfortable temperature and humidity levels. Key Features and Technology of the Bullet Train The B28 will also offer a Wi-Fi-based infotainment system with preloaded entertainment content. LCD screens will showcase passenger information in English, Hindi and regional languages. Public announcement systems and emergency communication units will permit passengers to get relevant updates and contact train staff. Bharat's first bullet train is BEING BUILT! 🇮🇳🚅 📍BEML facility, Bengaluru, Karnataka https://t.co/LAgeuFD9y9 — Piyush Goyal (@PiyushGoyal) November 1, 2026 Another highlight feature of the bullet train is accessibility. The train will have level boarding, retractable footsteps, wheelchair-friendly doors, specialised seating and toilet facilities for Divyangjan passengers. Braille signage will also help visually impaired travellers. To ensure smoother and quieter journeys, the train integrates sound insulation, noise-damping coatings and specially curated aerodynamic components. Its streamlined body can lower air resistance, turbulence and pressure changes, especially while passing through tunnels. The train will function on a 25 kV AC traction system and showcase regenerative braking technology, which recovers energy during braking to bolster efficiency. The B28 embodies an integral milestone in India's railway modernisation bid, and its integration on the Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor will be a crucial step towards building a modern, indigenous high-speed rail network. Passengers Accessibility for Mumbai-Ahmedabad Bullet Train To make the train accessible for everyone, its floor is aligned with the platform height to facilitate level boarding and will come with retractable steps integrated into the doors to help minimise the horizontal gap between the train and platform. Bullet Train Fare The ticket fare for India's maiden bullet train on the Mumbai–Ahmedabad route is slated to start at a minimum of ₹250 for short distances and reach approximately ₹3,000 for the full journey.

articles.title: Kuno Cheetah CCB-4 Enters Rajasthan's Baran Forest Area - GKToday
articles.content: Home Kuno Cheetah CCB-4 Enters Rajasthan’s Baran Forest Area Kuno Cheetah CCB-4 Enters Rajasthan’s Baran Forest Area November 2, 2026 Current Affairs Today - Latest Current Affairs - 2026-2027 Male cheetah CCB-4 travelled from Madhya Pradesh’s Kuno National Park into the forests of Baran district, Rajasthan, on Friday night. By 1 November 2026, he was in the Anjaronda forest area of the Kelwara range, Deputy Conservator of Forests Vivekanand Manikrao confirmed. Route and monitoring CCB-4 covered about 16 kilometres, crossing from Kurkuta village in Madhya Pradesh to Kurkuti in Rajasthan and moving through Dua, Silori and Khushiara before reaching Anjaronda. Wildlife teams from Kuno National Park and the Kelwara forest range are jointly tracking his movements in real time. Background and habitat About two-and-a-half to three years old, CCB-4 arrived from Botswana on 28 February 2026 as part of the third batch under Project Cheetah . In September, he formed an unusual hunting alliance with KNG-23, an India-born male; male cheetah coalitions typically consist of brothers. Baran’s open, semi-arid scrub and grasslands provide less-dense vegetation and prey such as chital, chinkara and young nilgai. Cheetahs KP-2 and KP-3, and female Veera with cub KPV-2, have also spent extended periods in the region; Veera and her cub returned to Kuno in late September 2026. Important Facts for Exams Range patterns: Female cheetahs are generally nomadic across large home ranges, whereas males are more sedentary and hold smaller territories with prey and access to females. Spot-based identification: Each cheetah has a distinctive coat-spot pattern that can be used to identify the individual. Hunting sequence: A cheetah stalks to within 30–200 metres, then charges, trips its prey with a dewclaw and kills it with a throat bite. articles.title: IIT Kanpur Patents Bamboo-Filled Vibration Barriers - GKToday
articles.content: Home IIT Kanpur Patents Bamboo-Filled Vibration Barriers IIT Kanpur Patents Bamboo-Filled Vibration Barriers November 2, 2026 Current Affairs Today - Latest Current Affairs - 2026-2027 Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur developed underground bamboo-filled barriers to screen ground-borne vibrations from traffic, construction and industrial activity. The system, titled “A passive vibration screening arrangement with bamboo in-filled wave barriers”, was developed by Priyanka Ghosh and Sreyashrao Surapreddi of the Department of Civil Engineering. The supplied dates differ: the technology is described as patented on 2 November 2026, while the Indian patent details give grant date 3 July 2023, patent number 436990, to S. Surapreddi and P. Ghosh. Design and research The barriers are installed in underground trenches to interrupt vibration transmission before it reaches vulnerable structures. The design is intended to be eco-friendly, cost-effective, and easy to install, dismantle and reinstall. Its stated advantages include reducing soil sloughing, eliminating sand pockets and limiting trench collapse. IIT Kanpur has made the technology available for licensing; suitability depends on ground conditions and vibration characteristics. A study in the Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering appeared in October 2024. Research published in the ISET Journal of Earthquake Technology in March 2025 reported satisfactory performance, particularly at higher frequencies. Important Facts for Exams Wave transmission: Vibrations travel as mechanical waves, and some mechanical linkages conduct them more efficiently than others. Passive mechanism: Passive vibration isolation uses materials and mechanical linkages to absorb and damp mechanical waves. Active isolation: Active isolation instead uses sensors and actuators to generate interference that cancels incoming vibration. articles.title: NTPC to set up India's first ceramic-based project to generate solar power at night in ... - Rajasthan
articles.content: Technology 1 min read NTPC to set up India's first ceramic-based project to generate solar power at night in Rajasthan's Bhadla NTPC will test a 320 kW ceramic thermal storage pilot at Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan to see if solar power can be generated after sunset. The project, approved by Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Limited, is intended to evaluate an alternative to battery storage and could shape future solar deployments if it works. ETRajasthan Updated On Nov 2, 2026 at 11:03 AM IST Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Limited (RRECL) has approved NTPC to set up a 320 kW pilot concentrated solar power (CSP) project at Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan . The project will test ceramic-based thermal energy storage technology to generate electricity using solar energy stored during the day, including after sunset. The project aims to assess the possibility of generating solar power at night while reducing dependence on conventional battery storage. Electricity generated through the pilot project will be used for internal and auxiliary consumption at the NTPC plant. Under the proposed technology, solar energy captured during the day will be stored as heat in high-temperature ceramic modules. After sunset, the stored heat will be used to operate an air turbine and generate electricity. The project will use ceramic thermal energy storage technology developed by US-based company 247Solar . NTPC is working with RRECL to implement and test the technology at Bhadla. Following the approval, preliminary feasibility studies, site surveys and structural testing will be undertaken at the project site. Solar power generation after sunset remains a challenge because conventional solar photovoltaic plants depend on sunlight and require storage systems to supply electricity after generation hours. The pilot project will assess whether thermal storage using ceramic modules can provide an alternative to chemical battery-based storage. If the technology proves feasible, it could be considered for deployment at other solar power projects. The pilot will also provide data on its operational performance and suitability for integration with existing solar infrastructure.
